judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long string of 'Whereas' recitals full of aspirational and open-textured language ('regional assets', 'greatest benefits', 'most efficient service in the public welfare') with no operative bite of its own. The vagueness is characteristic of preambles and rarely produces a nameable ambiguous term standing alone.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This is the classic recital-versus-operative-text situation: the preamble's sweeping account of what the 'comprehensive plan administered by a basin wide agency' will do is routinely invoked to expand or contract the operative reach of Sections 1.2(g), 3.8 and 13.1, and courts construing the compact's scope reach for it. That mismatch between broad purposive recital and the narrower operative definitions gives a court something real to construe.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare short-title clause; the only defect is a doubled period after 'Short title..', which changes nothing. No term carries competing meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Section 1.2(c) defining 'Compact' as Part I of this act, though 'this Act' versus 'compact' is used loosely across the instrument. Nothing operative turns on it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definitional preamble whose only soft edge is the escape hatch 'except as may be otherwise required by the context', which by design lets defined terms float. That escape clause is itself a lever an advocate could pull.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It governs every defined term, including the heavily contested 'project' in 1.2(g); the 'unless the context otherwise requires' formula is exactly what a party would cite to escape the definition in Section 3.8. Still, standing alone it creates no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Area of drainage into the Delaware River and its tributaries' is a hydrologically determinate boundary; 'including Delaware Bay' resolves the one doubtful case. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with Section 2.7 (commission acts 'within the limits of the basin') and 11.3. No conflicting definition elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure naming definition tied to Section 2.1. Nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.1 creates exactly this body; no other provision uses 'commission' differently, save the lower-case references to state water resources commissions in the New York sections, which are contextually clear.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Compact shall mean Part I of this act' is a simple mapping, though 'this act' shifts meaning depending on which of the five enacting statutes is read. That latent referential slippage is minor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Part II contains five different enacting 'Acts', and Section 15.1 repeatedly distinguishes 'this Act' from 'the Compact'; the definition thus does real work but also sits awkwardly across the five enactments. The tension is theoretical rather than operative.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Net induced adverse effects, whether or not compensated for' is genuinely vague — it has no measurable boundary, and 'commitment' as a species of expenditure is odd. A cost-allocation fight would turn on those words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds Sections 11.4, 13.3 and 15.1(a), which speak of cost allocation and apportionment without cross-referencing the definition; nothing squarely contradicts it. Fit is loose but not incoherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A sprawling definition ending in the catch-all 'or to facilitate any other uses of any of them', preceded by long enumerated specifics — the paradigm general-versus-specific problem, and 'necessary, useful or convenient' has no boundary. 'Facility' is also embedded in the contested 'project' definition, so its reach matters.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interlocks with 1.2(g) ('any separate facility undertaken... within a specified area') so that the breadth of 'facility' directly drives the scope of Section 3.8 review, and Sections 4.5 and 9.3 then carve back out ('shall not be construed to authorize... distributing water'). Those carve-backs suggest the drafters themselves feared the definition swept too far.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any appropriate branch, department, bureau or division thereof, as the case may be' is circular — 'appropriate' is undefined and does the work. Mild but nameable vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1 repeatedly allocates powers among the President, Congress and specific agencies without reference to this definition, but nothing contradicts it. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is the definition a federal court had to construe: 'any work, service or activity which is separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission, or any separate facility... for the conservation, utilization, control, development or management of water resources' is grammatically and substantively ambiguous — it is unclear whether 'identified by the commission' modifies all three verbs, whether the purposive clause limits 'work, service or activity' as well as 'facility', and whether a purely private extractive activity qualifies. Two reasonable readings, drastically different in scope, sit on the same words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its reach is only intelligible read against Section 3.8's 'substantial effect on the water resources of the basin', Section 1.5's promise to preserve existing state agencies, Section 3.6(b)'s enumerated standards, and the preamble's list of subjects — and those provisions pull in opposite directions on whether private, non-water-supply activity is a 'project'. Reading the instrument as a whole does not dissolve the tension; it sharpens it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A closed, exhaustive list of four states plus the federal government; no catch-all, no vague term. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Because 'signatory party' includes the federal government, Section 12.8's exemption of bonds from 'all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties' collides with Section 15.1(f), which denies federal tax exemption. This definition is the hinge of that conflict, though the defect lies more in 12.8.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Water and related natural resources in, on, under, or above the ground, including related uses of land, which are subject to beneficial use, ownership or control' turns on the undefined and elastic word 'related' — twice — and 'related uses of land' could swallow almost any land use. A court deciding what activities affect 'water resources' must construe this.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the operative measure in Section 3.8 ('substantial effect on the water resources of the basin'), in 3.6(b), and in the Article 11 rules, so its breadth is contested wherever the commission's regulatory reach is contested. Section 14.19's saving of riparian rights and Section 1.5's preservation of state agencies pull the other way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare introductory phrase to a set of legislative findings; nothing to construe on its own face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It labels what follows as 'find and declare' — findings, not operative commands — which is exactly the recital/operative fault line that matters when 1.3(e)'s purposes are used to expand Section 3.8. The introduction itself contributes little.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A declaratory finding using broad but non-operative language ('affected with a local, state, regional and national interest'). No enumerated list, no catch-all to fight over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: As a finding it can be marshalled against operative limits like Section 1.5 and 14.19, but standing alone it does not contradict any operative term. Modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Declares a purpose of 'joint exercise of such powers of sovereignty'; abstract, but no term whose boundary must be fixed to decide anything.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits comfortably with Section 1.4 (reserving congressional powers) and 5.5 (reserving state pollution authority), which qualify the 'joint exercise'. No genuine inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A finding that a single administrative agency is 'essential'; rhetorical rather than operative, with no term whose meaning is disputed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says a single agency is essential, while Sections 1.5, 5.5, 10.8, 11.1(c) and 11.2(c) all preserve the authority of existing federal and state agencies — a finding that points one way against operative text pointing another. That is a live recital-versus-operative tension a party would exploit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A factual prediction from 1961 ('ample to meet all presently projected demands'), and a run-on sentence joining two unrelated ideas without punctuation. The mechanical looseness does not change any obligation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The finding that water is 'ample' sits uneasily with Article 10's elaborate machinery for shortage, protected areas and drought emergencies, but that is a difference in register, not an operative conflict. Modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A list of purposes ending with the sweeping 'apply the principle of equal and uniform treatment to all water users who are similarly situated' — 'similarly situated' is undefined and would have to be construed if invoked. Otherwise the language is hortatory.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This purposes clause is the standard lever for reading Section 3.8 and the 1.2(g) 'project' definition broadly or narrowly, and it is in tension with Section 1.5's preservation of existing agencies and 14.19's saving of riparian rights. Courts construing the compact's regulatory reach reach for this text.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two saving sentences using conventional formulae ('nothing... shall be construed to relinquish', 'in derogation of'); the scope of 'any navigable waters within the basin' is settled federal usage. Little to fix.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly incorporated by Section 11.1 ('subject in each case to the provisions of Section 1.4'), by 15.1(b)'s proviso and by 15.1(t), which makes the United States' membership contingent on this section's validity — heavy cross-traffic, but all of it deliberate. The relationships are coordinated, not conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To the extent not inconsistent with the compact' and 'to the fullest extent it finds feasible and advantageous' are both open-ended, and the section both states a purpose and gives a directive without saying which controls. A party resisting commission jurisdiction would name 'not inconsistent' as the ambiguous hinge.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It promises to preserve existing state and federal offices, which runs against Section 3.8's blanket submission requirement, Section 10.8's supersession of state permits, and Section 1.3(c)'s 'single administrative agency' finding. It is also expressly incorporated by 7.4(b) and 8.2(b), so its meaning propagates.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The renewal window — 'not later than 20 years nor sooner than 25 years prior to the termination' — is expressed in an inverted, counter-intuitive order that invites misreading, and 'none of the signatory states' excludes the federal government without saying so. The window is workable but the drafting is a trap.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates with 1.6(b) and with Section 15.1(q)'s reserved congressional right to repeal, which could end federal participation without triggering this clause. That gap is real but was addressed by 15.1(t).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short wind-up clause that defers wholly to 'act of the Congress'; no term needs construing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leaves dissolution mechanics to Congress even though the states may terminate under 1.6(a), and it says nothing about bondholders' rights under 12.18 and 12.19. A latent gap, but not a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Body politic and corporate... as an agency and instrumentality of the governments of the respective signatory parties' is standard compact language, but the dual federal-and-state characterisation is exactly the kind of hybrid status that gets litigated. Still, no single ambiguous term drives an outcome here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It calls the commission an instrumentality of all signatory parties including the United States, while Section 15.1(m) directs that for FTCA and Tucker Act purposes 'the commission shall not be considered a Federal agency' and 15.1(n) denies federal-employee status to its staff. That is a genuine characterisation conflict a litigant would press.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'One commissioner to be appointed by the President... to serve during the term of office of the President' is a definite term of service; the phrase is clear on its face. No lexical problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The compact's own Endnote states flatly that 'Sections 2.2 and 15.1(d) were inconsistent as to the term of the federal representative's appointment' — a conflict so real that Congress repealed 15.1(d) to fix it, and WRDA 2007 then displaced 2.2 again. This is a named, documented internal contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Detailed and internally consistent: appointment, term, removal at pleasure, and vacancy filling are each addressed. 'Unless otherwise provided by law of the signatory party' is a clean deferral.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(d) made the federal alternate serve at the President's pleasure notwithstanding Article 2, and New York § 631 supplies a further substitute if both member and alternate are absent — layered, but the notwithstanding language sequences them. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Serve without compensation but may be reimbursed for necessary expenses' is a familiar and workable formula; 'necessary' is a common standard courts apply routinely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(r) provides that 'the provisions of Sections 2.4 and 2.6... notwithstanding', the federal member may be paid compensation by the United States — a direct exception, but one drafted as an express override rather than a conflict. New York § 631(2) adds its own reimbursement source.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A majority of the membership' is precise (a majority of five, not of those present), and the one-vote rule is flat. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Several provisions require unanimity instead — 3.3(a) emergency action, 3.5(c)-(d) consent of decree parties, and 13.3(b)(2)'s 'unanimous vote' apportionment — but each is an express carve-out from the majority default. Coordinated, not contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Straightforward self-organisation powers with a definite annual officer election; no vague operative term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(r) overrides it as to compensation of the federal member's advisor, and New York § 632 designates the mayor of New York City as its advisor — both are supplements contemplated by the 'in his discretion' language. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Whenever such action may be necessary or convenient to effectuate its powers' is elastic, and the final sentence's 'such power' is ambiguous as to whether the consent requirement covers only the extraterritorial acts or the sale of water too. The referent of 'such power' is a nameable problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be squared with 1.2(e), which defines 'facility' to include property 'within or without the basin', and with 3.6(a)'s unrestricted power to own and operate facilities; the consent-of-the-state condition here is the only brake. That interaction is workable but contested at the edges.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three mandatory but wholly general sentences ('shall develop and effectuate plans, policies and projects'); the language is aspirational rather than boundary-drawing. Nothing here needs a definition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states the commission's mission in terms that Articles 3 through 13 then specify, and it is a natural source for arguing that commission powers are broader than the enumerated ones. But there is no operative provision it contradicts.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare directive to formulate and adopt three documents 'in accordance with Article 13'. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article 13 restates the same three obligations in different words — 13.2 fixes 'six years' where 3.2(b) says only 'such reasonably foreseeable period' — so the two articles duplicate each other imperfectly. The cross-reference here is what makes that duplication visible.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Comprehensive plan... for the immediate and long range development and uses of the water resources' — 'immediate and long range' is loose, but the paragraph is a direction to adopt, not a standard to apply.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It differs from Section 13.1 in consultation requirements (here 'water users and interested public bodies'; 13.1 adds 'public utilities' and requires public hearings), a small mismatch between two statements of the same duty. Nothing irreconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'For such reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine' delegates the horizon entirely to the commission, and 'all public and private projects affecting the basin' is very broad without a threshold. The absence of any 'substantial effect' qualifier here is notable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 13.2 covers the same water resources program but fixes 'the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period', and Section 3.8's approval trigger is limited to projects of 'substantial effect' while this paragraph sweeps in 'all public and private projects affecting the basin'. That mismatch in threshold is a real handle for argument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain requirement of two budgets consistent with the water resources program. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 13.3 elaborates the same budgets and adds the apportionment and certification machinery; no inconsistency between them. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'In accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment' imports an entire body of contested judicial doctrine as the operative standard, and 'as need appears' is unbounded. Both are nameable open terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The allocation power granted here is immediately hemmed in by 3.3(a)-(c), 3.4 and 3.5, and 3.3(b) says allocations are not 'an apportionment of the waters of the basin among the parties' even though the power is granted 'in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment'. That is close to saying the commission may apportion but its apportionment is not an apportionment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long single sentence with a proviso that reverses the rule in emergencies; 'impair, diminish or otherwise adversely affect' is a broad catch-all after two specifics, and 'catastrophe' is undefined. The unanimity requirement appears twice with different referents (parties to the decree, then members of the commission), which is easy to conflate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with 3.4, 3.5 and New York § 633, which conditions New York's consent on prior approval of its water resources commission; the interlocking consents are intricate but deliberate. The emergency proviso, however, sits in tension with 3.5's flat prohibition on impairing the decree.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The proviso preserving power 'to enter into covenants with respect to water supply' is a sizeable exception carved from a flat prohibition, and 'a benefit or development of the water resources' reads as a drafting slip for 'the benefit'. The relationship between the rule and its proviso is genuinely unclear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It denies that allocations constitute an 'apportionment' while 3.3's opening invokes 'the doctrine of equitable apportionment', and the covenant power it preserves can outlast any particular allocation. That internal pull is the kind courts have to resolve.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any proper party deeming itself aggrieved' leaves 'proper party' undefined, and the split between de novo Supreme Court review for out-of-basin diversions and ordinary review elsewhere turns on the undefined phrase 'out-of-basin diversion'. Both are nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It creates a second review track alongside 3.8's and 10.6's 'judicial review in any court of competent jurisdiction' and alongside 15.1(p)'s grant of original federal district court jurisdiction, and New York § 634 defines the phrase differently again for different sections. Multiple overlapping review provisions invite argument about which governs.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A dense waiver with two nested exceptions, one of which ('to effectuate rights, powers, duties and obligations under Section 3.3') nearly swallows the waiver, since 3.3 is the very allocation power. The double 'increase or decrease' and the exception's asymmetry (only increases) invite construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with 3.3(a) and 3.5, the waiver is qualified by the same emergency and consent machinery, and New York § 633 layers a state-law consent requirement on top. The Section 3.3 exception makes the relationship between the waiver and the allocation power circular.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Nothing in this compact shall be construed in any way to impair, diminish or otherwise adversely affect' is a broad saving clause, and 'To this end, and without limitation thereto' signals the list that follows is illustrative — the classic general-versus-specific setup. But the drafting flags this expressly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It begins 'Except as specifically provided in Sections 3.3 and 3.4', yet 3.3(a) permits the commission to alter decree diversions in an emergency, so the exception and the prohibition overlap. Also relevant to 14.14(a)'s carve-out for property connected to decree diversions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Impede or interfere with' is broad but familiar; the paragraph is a flat prohibition with no list to construe against. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It flatly bars any action interfering with the decree, while 3.3(a) allows exactly such interference on unanimous emergency consent — the 'Except as specifically provided' opener in 3.5 is the only reconciler. Workable but contested.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any fee, charge or assessment with respect to diversions... permitted by said decree' is definite and closed. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits alongside 3.7 (rates and charges), 4.3 (assessable improvements), 11.3 (reserved state taxing powers) and 15.1(b), which independently bars charges on pre-existing lawful withdrawals — a stack of overlapping charge prohibitions whose combined boundary is unclear. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single long clause listing planning, design, construction, operation and control of projects, structures or facilities — specific enough, but 'used in connection with' withdrawals authorised by the decree is elastic. Nameable but modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It withdraws jurisdiction over decree-related facilities, which cuts directly against Section 3.8's requirement that every project of substantial effect be submitted and approved; 3.8's own 'subject to the provisions of Sections 3.3 and 3.5' is the reconciling text. Deliberate sequencing.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One short sentence with a single condition. Nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.3(a)'s reference to consulting 'the river master under said decree'. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The commission may:' — a bare stem. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The permissive 'may' here contrasts with the mandatory 'shall' of 3.1, 3.9 and 8.3, a distinction that matters where a duty is asserted. Otherwise unremarkable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long verb-string ending in 'determined by the commission to be necessary, convenient or useful for the purposes of this compact' — an entirely self-referential standard, and 'activities and services' is broader than the defined 'project'. The self-judging qualifier is the nameable soft spot.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It grants power over 'projects, facilities, properties, activities and services' whereas 1.2(g) defines 'project' more narrowly, and 15.1(a) forbids the commission from taking any project beyond the planning stage without congressional authorisation. That federal reservation directly qualifies this grant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All projects and facilities in the basin which affect its water resources, including without limitation thereto' followed by six enumerated examples — the express 'without limitation' disclaims ejusdem generis, but the enumerated items (water treatment plants, trunk mains, flood works) are all conventional water infrastructure, which invites the argument that the general words take colour from them. That is exactly the general-versus-specific dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This standards power reaches projects that merely 'affect' water resources, a lower threshold than Section 3.8's 'substantial effect', and the enumerated list has been used to argue that 'project' in 1.2(g) means water-infrastructure works. The two thresholds and the two lists must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Research and data powers, expressly 'including without limitation thereto' a list of technical topics; permissive and non-regulatory, so little turns on the boundary. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Complements 3.6(e) and 13.1's information gathering; nothing contradicts it. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Publicize such information when and as needed for... other purposes' ends an enumerated list with an open catch-all, though nothing coercive rides on it. Minor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps with 6.4's flood warning and posting power and 14.12's reporting power without conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such special ground water investigations... as may be required to formulate and administer the comprehensive plan' is self-limiting by reference to the plan. Definite enough.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 13.1 and 3.6(c); no competing provision. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A publication power framed around 'the water problems of the basin' and 'the needs, resources and policies of the basin' — general but non-operative language nobody would need construed. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits beside 14.12's annual reporting duty without conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such loans, grants, services or other aids as may be lawfully available from public or private sources' ends in a catch-all after three specifics, and 'as the commission may deem necessary or desirable' is self-judging. Modest but nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps with 12.20(c) and 14.1(a)(2) and 14.13, which grant the same receipt-of-funds power in different words, and with 15.1(e)'s reservation over federal appropriations. Duplication rather than contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such other and different powers as may be delegated... and... all powers necessary or convenient to carry out its express powers or which may be reasonably implied therefrom' is a pure catch-all closing a long enumerated list of specific powers — the textbook general-versus-specific problem, and 'reasonably implied' has no boundary. A party resisting commission authority would fight over exactly this.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against 14.1(a)(6) ('all corporate powers essential to the declared objects'), 1.5's preservation of existing agencies and 15.1(o)'s refusal to enlarge federal authority, the implied-powers clause is the mechanism by which the enumerated limits could be bypassed. That is a whole-instrument tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A rate-setting power with procedural conditions; 'rates, rentals, charges and tolls and classifications thereof' is enumerated and the 'without regulation or control by any... agency of any signatory party' clause is emphatic and clear. Little vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(b) expressly cuts back this section — no charge for withdrawals lawfully free at the effective date and none on commercial navigation — and Section 11.3 reserves state taxing powers over the same withdrawals, so three provisions govern the same charges. The federal reservation is drafted as an override, which limits the conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No project having a substantial effect on the water resources of the basin' turns on two open terms — the defined but contested 'project' and the wholly undefined 'substantial effect' — and the second sentence sets an approval standard ('substantially impair or conflict with the comprehensive plan') that is a different test again. This is the provision whose reach a federal court had to decide.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its scope depends entirely on 1.2(g) and 1.2(i), it must be squared with 3.3 and 3.5 (expressly), with 11.1(b) and 11.2(b), which bar expenditure on any project not already in the comprehensive plan, and with 1.5's promise to preserve existing state agencies. Those provisions cannot all be given full effect simultaneously, which is precisely the contested ground.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To this end, but with limitation thereto, the commission may:' is a plain mechanical error — the parallel provisions (3.5, 3.6(b), 4.1) all read 'without limitation thereto', so the missing 'out' inverts the meaning from illustrative to exhaustive. A mistake in writing that changes what the provision means is squarely a Category 1.2 defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against 4.1 and 3.5, which use the correct 'without limitation thereto' formula, the error makes 3.9's list look closed while its siblings are open — an inconsistency across the instrument produced by the slip. The error is nameable and its effect on the enumerated list in (a)-(d) is real.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Advise, consult, contract, financially assist, or otherwise cooperate with any and all such agencies' — the residual 'or otherwise cooperate' after four specifics, but the power is permissive and cooperative rather than coercive. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Governed by the flawed 'but with limitation thereto' stem in 3.9, which affects whether this list is exhaustive. Otherwise consistent with 11.5.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Or for any other purpose' is an unbounded catch-all closing a list of specific engineering functions — a genuine ejusdem generis question if the commission ever used it to employ an agency for something unrelated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It permits employing signatory agencies generally, which sits with 1.5's directive to use existing agencies 'to the fullest extent'; New York § 637 independently limits what state agencies may accept. Coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'So far as consistent with the comprehensive plan' is a qualifier of degree without a test, and 'permit the decentralized administration thereof' is undefined. Moderate softness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 13.1 and 1.5's decentralisation policy, and with 7.4(b)/8.2(b)'s preference for other operators. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A narrow qualifying power tied to identified federal legislation; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits with 3.6(g) and 12.20(c); 15.1(o) limits enlargement of other federal agencies' authority but not this. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An enumerated list of possible committee constituencies introduced by 'may be comprised of', which is expressly non-exhaustive and non-binding. Nothing turns on the boundary.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Distinct from the single advisor of 2.6 and New York § 632's advisory committee; no conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To this end, without limitation thereto' expressly opens the list, and 'such off-river sites as it may find appropriate' is self-judging, but the powers granted are conventional and concrete. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It grants power to develop water supply projects, while 4.5 forbids the commission to 'engage in the business of distributing water' and 15.1(a) bars any project beyond planning without an Act of Congress. Those limits qualify but do not contradict this grant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long list of purposes ending in the bare catch-all 'and other purposes', and 'the prevention of undue salinity' uses the undefined qualifier 'undue'. Both are nameable Category 1 features.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with 3.3's allocation limits, 3.5's decree protections and 4.2(b)'s prohibition on diminishing augmented flow; the storage-and-release power is bounded by the decree provisions. Moderate interaction, no clear conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A negative covenant on signatory parties with three enumerated exceptions; 'permit any augmentation of flow to be diminished' is awkward but its sense is recoverable. The obligation is to prevent third-party diversions, which is a demanding duty stated obliquely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It imposes a duty on states to police diversions, which must be squared with 10.3's grandfathering of permits 'heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states' and 10.8's supersession rule. The exception 'duly authorized by this compact' does much of the reconciling work.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Specially benefited thereby to a measurable extent' and the proviso that 'no such assessment shall exceed the actual benefit' set up a valuation standard that is inherently contestable, and 'the procedure prescribed by law for local improvement assessments' does not say whose law. Both are nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It permits assessments on water users while 3.5(b) bars charges on decree-permitted diversions, 11.3 reserves state taxing power over the same withdrawals, and 15.1(b) bars charges on withdrawals lawfully free in 1961. Four provisions govern the same money.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Review and consider all existing rights, plans and programs... which are pertinent' — 'pertinent' is the only soft word, and the hearing requirement is definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its 'public hearing on each proposed project' duty overlaps 14.4(b), which lists the occasions requiring hearings and adds 'in all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing'. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The prohibition on engaging 'in the business of distributing water' is undefined at its edge — providing 'transmission facilities' and distributing water are hard to separate, and the same sentence grants the one and forbids the other. That internal juxtaposition is a genuine ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels 9.3's ban on 'direct sale to consumers' while 2.7 authorises the commission 'to sell or dispose of water... within or without the basin' and 14.4(b) contemplates contracts for the sale of water resources. Reconciling wholesale sale with a ban on distribution is not obvious.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Control potential pollution and abate or dilute existing pollution' is standard regulatory phrasing; 'invoke as complainant the power and jurisdiction of' state agencies is unusual but its sense is clear. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with 5.2 through 5.4 and is preserved against federal displacement by 15.1(k). No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The operative standard — pollution 'shall not injuriously affect waters of the basin as contemplated by the comprehensive plan' — uses the undefined 'injuriously affect' and makes the plan the yardstick, and the enumerated 'variable factors' close with 'usage of the waters affected'. A polluter and the commission could read this very differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The commission 'may assume jurisdiction' only when the plan 'so requires', which makes 13.1 the trigger, while 5.5 preserves every signatory's independent authority and 15.1(k) preserves federal water-pollution functions. Layered jurisdiction over the same discharges.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A covenant to reach a condition described by a chain of qualitative standards — 'satisfactory condition', 'after reasonable treatment', 'free from unsightly or malodorous nuisances' — none of which has a boundary, and 'agrees to enact any necessary legislation' is an obligation of uncertain enforceability. Rich in nameable vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It obliges states to legislate while 5.5 says nothing in the compact repeals or qualifies state authority and 15.1(k) preserves federal functions; whether this covenant is enforceable against a legislature is a whole-instrument question. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A detailed enforcement provision with defined triggers and remedies; 'a reasonable time for the construction of any necessary works' is the only soft term and courts apply such standards routinely. Comparatively tight.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'The courts of the signatory parties shall have jurisdiction' overlaps 15.1(p)'s grant of original federal jurisdiction and removal, and New York § 634 defines 'court of competent jurisdiction' for that state. Overlapping but not contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A saving clause using the familiar 'nothing... shall be construed to repeal, modify or qualify'; the words 'additional conditions and restrictions to lessen or prevent' confine it to more-stringent state action, which is a clear one-way ratchet. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves state pollution authority while 1.3(c) declares a 'single administrative agency' essential, 10.8 supersedes conflicting state permits, and New York § 641 makes inconsistent state law inapplicable — the last flatly the reverse of this section's premise. That is a nameable cross-instrument tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'As it may deem necessary or desirable' and 'in such manner, at such times, and under such regulations as the commission may deem appropriate' are wholly self-judging, but the subject matter (flood facilities) is concrete. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The power to store and release waters overlaps 4.2(a) and is constrained by 3.3(a) and 3.5's decree protections. Coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Recommended standards' is an odd hybrid — the commission may 'adopt, amend and repeal' them, yet they are only recommendations, and the second sentence says states may adopt regulations 'not inconsistent therewith', which implies they bind after all. That internal tension over whether the standards are advisory or mandatory is a real ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 6.3 requires flood land acquisition to 'be in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2', treating them as operative, and 14.17's penal sanction reaches violations of 'any rule, regulation or order' — so whether recommended standards bind matters instrument-wide. Genuine.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Detailed hearing procedure with a clear sequence; 'standards for flood plain use which will safeguard the public health, safety and property' is broad but is a familiar police-power formula. Moderate-low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says hearings shall be held 'in the manner provided by Article 14', which points to 14.4(b); consistent. It also feeds 6.3 and New York § 636's technical-aid agreements.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Preventing unwarranted constrictions that reduce the ability of the river channel to carry flood water' uses the undefined 'unwarranted', and the purposes for acquisition are enumerated without a catch-all. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It requires action to 'be in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2', but 6.2(a) calls those standards merely 'recommended' — so the acquisition power is anchored to something the compact elsewhere describes as advisory. That is a specific, nameable mismatch.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Lands particularly subject to flood' and 'as conditions may warrant' are loose but the power is purely informational, so nothing coercive rides on the boundary. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps 3.6(d)'s publicity power without conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Shall promote sound practices of watershed management' is a duty stated so generally that it has no ascertainable content, but for that reason nobody would sue on it. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is a mandatory 'shall' where the rest of Article 7 is permissive 'may', a small mismatch in register between the article's opening duty and its operative powers. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A permissive list of soil and forestry activities; 'sound forestry practices' is undefined but non-operative. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Constrained by 7.4(b)'s requirement that no other suitable agency be available before the commission operates a facility. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Fish and wildlife habitats related to the water resources of the basin' uses 'related to', the same elastic connector as 1.2(i), but in a permissive grant. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Fits 1.2(i)'s definition of water resources as including 'related natural resources' and 7.4(b)'s operating limitation. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A cooperation duty in wholly general terms; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Identical in wording to 8.2(a), which is duplication rather than conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No other suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions' makes the commission judge of 'suitable' and 'reasonable', which is a real if modest ambiguity in a mandatory precondition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly tied to 'the intent and purpose expressed in Section 1.5', which itself is qualified by 'to the extent not inconsistent with the compact' — so the precondition inherits 1.5's softness, and 3.6(a) grants an unqualified power to operate projects. The two grants sit in tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Water related public sports and recreational facilities' — 'water related' is undefined and could be read narrowly or broadly, and 'shall provide for the development' is a mandatory duty with no measure of performance. Moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Expressly made 'subject to the provisions of Section 8.2', which bars operation where another agency is available; the mandatory duty and the operating bar coexist awkwardly but are sequenced. Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A general cooperation duty, word-for-word the same as 7.4(a). Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 7.4(a) exactly; duplication across articles, not conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Same 'suitable... upon reasonable conditions' judgment standard as 7.4(b), with the same modest softness. Moderate-low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with 8.1's mandatory duty to provide for development and 8.3(c)'s duty to administer facilities 'owned or controlled by the commission', the bar on operating creates a circularity about what the commission may actually run. Also anchored to the elastic Section 1.5.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Within limits prescribed by this article' is a vague internal cross-limit — the article contains no obvious express 'limits' other than 8.2(b). A small referential puzzle.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 'limits prescribed by this article' most naturally means 8.2(b)'s bar on operating, yet 8.3(c) then requires the commission to provide for administration, operation and maintenance of its facilities. That circularity is the same one flagged at 8.1 and 8.2(b).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A duty to 'encourage' and 'assist in the coordination'; unenforceably general but not ambiguous in any nameable way. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.9 and 8.2(a). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Recommend standards' — like 6.2(a), it leaves unclear whether recommended standards have any binding force, but here nothing else depends on them. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Parallels 6.2(a)'s 'recommended standards' without the complication that 6.3 creates there. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Owned or controlled by the commission' and 'in accordance with this article' are definite enough; the letting of concessions is governed in detail by 8.4. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It commands the commission to operate its recreational facilities while 8.2(b) forbids it to operate any such facility where another agency is available — a direct pull between two paragraphs of the same article. That is the kind of internal inconsistency courts must resolve.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A mandatory competitive bidding regime for concessions, including renewals and extensions; the requirements are concrete, with a typographical 'therefore' for 'therefor' that changes nothing. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(l) expressly disapplies this section to 'facilities operated pursuant to any other Federal law', a carve-out whose reach is unclear but which is drafted as an override. Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'May be impounded and used by or under authority of the commission... in accordance with the comprehensive plan' is a permissive grant tied to the plan; nothing ambiguous stands out. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be squared with 3.3 and 3.5's decree protections and with 15.1(a)'s requirement of congressional authorisation before any project proceeds beyond planning. Coordinated by express cross-references elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete power to develop and operate dams for hydroelectric generation. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 9.1, 9.4 and 3.6(a); the Federal Power Commission's jurisdiction is preserved generally by 1.4 and 15.1(s). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The section grants transmission facilities 'for the purpose of wholesale marketing of power' and in the same sentence forbids 'the business of direct sale to consumers' — the boundary between wholesale marketing and direct sale is exactly what a dispute would turn on, and 'where such facilities are not otherwise available upon reasonable terms' adds a second open condition. Two nameable soft terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels 4.5's ban on 'distributing water' while 2.7 authorises the commission to 'sell or dispose of water, hydroelectric power or other water resources within or without the basin' and 14.4(b) contemplates contracts for the sale of hydroelectric energy 'to any person, corporation or entity'. Squaring 'any person' with a ban on direct consumer sales is not straightforward.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'On reasonable terms, consideration and duration' is a triple reasonableness standard with no benchmark, though it governs the commission's own contracting discretion. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits with 9.2's power to 'authorize to be developed and operated' and 14.9's competitive bidding rules, which do not obviously apply to development contracts. That gap is minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonable, nondiscriminatory, and just' is a three-word standard with no content of its own — a short phrase that a ratepayer and the commission would read very differently, and which courts have historically had to construe in utility settings. Genuine vagueness in a very short provision.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.7 lets the commission fix rates 'without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party', which removes the usual regulator who would apply this standard; and 15.1(b) limits charges in other respects. Who enforces 'just and reasonable' is left unstated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such power or regulation or control' appears to be a slip for 'such power of regulation or control', a small mechanical error, and the delegation power is bounded only by 'as it may deem necessary or desirable'. Both are nameable if minor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York § 637 forbids state agencies to accept delegations they could not exercise independently, and 10.8 lets commission regulation supersede state permits — so delegation and supersession run in opposite directions over the same subject. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Have developed or threaten to develop to such a degree as to create a water shortage or to impair or conflict with the requirements or effectuation of the comprehensive plan' is a compound, wholly qualitative trigger, and 'protected areas' is defined only by that trigger. The termination duty then keys to 'such shortage', though the designation could rest on plan conflict rather than shortage — a mismatch between the entry and exit tests.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exit condition ('whenever it determines that such shortage no longer exists') does not cover the plan-conflict ground for designation, so an area designated on that ground has no stated termination trigger. That is a specific internal gap within the same section and against 10.3's permit regime.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two enumerated exceptions with no catch-all, and the quantity threshold is set by regulation; 'domestic, municipal, agricultural or industrial uses' is a closed list that arguably excludes other uses entirely. That expressio unius point is nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The grandfather in clause (ii) for permits 'heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states' is directly cut down by 10.8, which supersedes state permits 'to the extent of any conflict'. Those two provisions point in opposite directions on the same permits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Drought or other condition which may cause an actual and immediate shortage' pairs a specific with an open-ended residual, and the emergency ban reaches withdrawals 'for any purpose' — broader than 10.3's four enumerated uses. The mismatch in scope between the two sections is visible on the face of this one.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 10.3 grandfathers pre-existing state permits but 10.4 contains no such saving, and 3.3(a) has its own separate emergency machinery requiring unanimous consent and consultation with the river master. Two emergency regimes with different procedures govern overlapping facts.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The permit standard turns on avoiding depletion that 'will adversely affect the comprehensive plan or the just and equitable interests and rights of other lawful users', with a further instruction to 'balance and reconcile alternative and conflicting uses' — layered qualitative tests with no priority among them. A denied applicant would litigate exactly these words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It makes the comprehensive plan the yardstick, tying it to 13.1, while 3.3(b) says allocations confer no 'superiority of right' and 14.19 preserves riparian rights — so the 'just and equitable interests and rights of other lawful users' has no settled source. Moderate cross-instrument strain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Sections 10.3 through 10.5' is a clean range and 'court of competent jurisdiction' is a term of art. The only softness is that the phrase is left undefined by the compact itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York § 634 defines 'court of competent jurisdiction' differently for this very section (an Article 78 court) than for the compact generally, and 15.1(p) grants original federal district-court jurisdiction over all cases arising under the compact. Three provisions describe the reviewing forum, which invites argument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Each state shall provide for the maintenance and preservation of such records... as the commission shall prescribe' is a definite duty with content delegated to the commission. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It obliges 'each state' although 1.2(h) makes the federal government a 'signatory party' but not a 'state', so the federal government is silently excluded; consistent with 15.1's general federal reservations. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Whenever the commission finds it necessary or desirable to exercise the powers conferred by this article' is self-judging, and 'superseded to the extent of any conflict' leaves the boundary of supersession to be worked out case by case. Both nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supersedes exactly the state permits that 10.3(ii) expressly preserves, and it cuts against 1.5's preservation of existing agencies and 5.5's saving of state authority. This is a specific, identifiable clash with 10.3.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An introductory stem stating a purpose ('avoiding conflicts of jurisdiction') and making the rules 'subject in each case to the provisions of Section 1.4'. The stem itself is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Making federal project rules 'subject to' Section 1.4's reservation of congressional powers means the rules yield wherever Congress's navigation or commerce powers are engaged, which substantially undercuts (b); and 15.1(s) adds yet another layer of qualification. The stem is where those tensions are anchored.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All projects related to powers delegated to the commission' uses the elastic 'related to' and gives no content to 'consultation'. Modest but nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It applies to federal projects but is subject to 1.4 and to 15.1(s), which subordinates the whole scheme to federal constitutional authority and lets the President delete plan provisions. The consultation duty survives, but its bite is uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No expenditure or commitment shall be made... nor shall it be deemed authorized, unless it shall have first been included by the commission in the comprehensive plan' is a flat bar, but 'nor shall it be deemed authorized' purports to unauthorise congressionally authorised federal projects — a striking reach whose meaning is contestable. The added clause distinguishes it from 11.2(b) for no stated reason.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conditions all federal spending on plan inclusion while 1.4 reserves congressional power, 15.1(a) requires congressional authorisation of commission projects, and 15.1(s) allows the President to delete plan provisions and requires only that federal action 'not substantially conflict' with the plan. Those provisions cannot all be given literal effect together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A saving clause preserving existing federal agency authority 'except as specifically provided by this section'. Clear on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves federal agency authority in the same breath that (b) makes any expenditure unauthorised absent plan inclusion — the saving and the bar sit in the same three-paragraph section pointing opposite ways. That is a nameable internal inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An introductory stem parallel to 11.1 but without the 'subject to Section 1.4' qualifier; the omission is deliberate and the stem is clear. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It governs state and local projects while 1.5 preserves existing state agencies and 10.8 supersedes state permits — overlapping regimes, but the stem itself does not create the clash. Moderate-low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Word-for-word the same as 11.1(a), with the same elastic 'related to' and undefined 'consultation'. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 11.1(a) for state projects; consistent within the article. Low-moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No expenditure or commitment shall be made... unless it shall have first been included by the commission in the comprehensive plan' is a sweeping prohibition on state and local spending with no de minimis threshold and no exception. Its literal breadth is its problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.8 conditions projects on 'substantial effect' and approval, whereas this paragraph conditions all state and local project spending on prior plan inclusion — two different gates for the same activity — and 11.2(c) then preserves state agency authority. Harmonising the three is a genuine construction problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A saving clause for state and local agency authority 'except as specifically provided by this section'. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves state authority alongside (b)'s bar on any expenditure not in the plan, and alongside 10.8's supersession and New York § 641's disapplication of inconsistent state law. The saving and the bar pull against each other within one section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A reservation of state taxing power measured by withdrawal or diversion, limited to use 'within the jurisdictions of the respective signatory parties'. Concrete.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reserves state charges on the same withdrawals that 3.5(b) forbids the commission to charge, that 4.3 lets the commission assess, and that 15.1(b) protects from charge altogether — and 14.3 exempts the commission itself from state taxation. Several charge regimes overlap on one subject.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Uniform standards and procedures' and 'equitable cost sharing and reimbursement formulas' are broad but are directives to create rules rather than rules themselves. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It anchors 12.20(a)'s cost-sharing plan and 13.3's apportionment, and 15.1(a) requires congressional review of cost apportionment for federal projects. Coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Uniform and consistent procedures for the allocation of project costs' — abstract but not ambiguous in any operative way. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Uses 'cost' as defined in 1.2(d), which includes the vague 'net induced adverse effects'; that imported vagueness is the only real interaction. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A list of arrangements to be developed; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Feeds 12.20(a) and 14.13; consistent. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An accounting-system directive; concrete and administrative. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 14.11's audit provisions and 13.3's budget machinery. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Payments in lieu of taxes' is defined operationally in 14.3, not here, and 'determining the basis and apportioning amounts' is left open. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.3 already fixes the in-lieu payment formula (equal to taxes for the year before acquisition, for ten years), so this paragraph's grant of discretion to apportion in-lieu payments overlaps a prescribed formula. A small but real doubling.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two obligations in one sentence — the commission 'shall furnish' services, each party 'pledges itself to provide' services 'within the limits of available appropriations' — with the appropriations proviso arguably attaching to both. The final 'may be reimbursable whenever the parties deem appropriate' leaves cost allocation wholly open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(h) expressly overrides this section for the United States, reducing the federal pledge to whatever agencies agree or the President directs, and New York § 638 restates the state pledge; so the mutual pledge is asymmetric in practice. The override is drafted deliberately.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The section says bonds are 'payable solely out of the properties and revenues of the commission without recourse to taxation' and in the next breath that they are 'direct and general obligations of the commission' with 'the full faith and credit of the commission' pledged — those two characterisations sit uneasily together and a bondholder and the commission would read them differently. That internal juxtaposition is a nameable ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with 12.3 (no power to pledge any signatory's credit) and 12.18 (a first and exclusive lien on identified revenues), the 'full faith and credit' pledge has no clear content beyond the commission's own assets. The three provisions must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The opening — 'The purpose of this compact shall include without limitation thereto all costs of any project' — is a mechanical oddity: a section headed 'Funds and Expenses' that redefines 'the purpose of this compact' as a list of costs. Read literally it is close to nonsense and plainly means 'purposes for which bonds may be issued'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The phrase 'purposes of this compact' recurs throughout (1.5, 3.6(a), 12.1, 14.1), so a provision purporting to enlarge that phrase to cover bond issuance costs has instrument-wide reach it cannot have been meant to have. That mismatch is genuine.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A flat exclusion of signatory and municipal credit plus a personal-immunity sentence; both are definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.20(b) permits bonds to be sold 'with or without the guaranty of such signatory party', which is in tension with the flat statement that the commission may not 'impose any obligation for payment of the bonds upon any signatory party'. The guaranty is voluntary, which mostly reconciles them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A detailed refunding power; 'duplicate interest' is unusual but the mechanics are conventional and specific. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'All provisions of this compact applicable to the issuance of bonds are applicable to refunding bonds' incorporates 12.7's fifty-year maturity cap and 12.13's bidding requirements, which is coherent. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long but precise: authorisation by resolution, non-dependence of validity on proceeds or completion, series, security, denominations, redemption. Conventional bond-law drafting.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 12.6, 12.13 and 12.18; 12.20(b)'s 'notwithstanding any other provision' carve-out for private placement is expressly reconciled. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Very long, but the one interesting phrase — covenants 'other than any restriction on the regulatory powers vested in the commission by this compact' — draws a clear line, and the rest is a standard indenture catalogue. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The bar on covenanting away regulatory powers protects Articles 5 and 10, yet 12.18 makes pledged revenues a trust fund that cannot be used for other purposes — a mild constraint on rate-setting under 3.7 and 9.5. Reconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No bond or its terms shall mature in more than fifty years from its own date' is awkwardly phrased ('or its terms' adds nothing) but the fifty-year cap and the per-bond calculation rule are numerically definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 12.4's application of all issuance provisions to refunding bonds and with the compact's 100-year duration in 1.6(a). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Free and exempt from all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties, except for transfer, inheritance and estate taxes' is definite on its face; the enumerated exceptions are closed. The trouble is not vagueness but reach.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.2(h) makes the federal government a 'signatory party', so this exempts bonds from federal taxation — which 15.1(f) squarely denies, permitting federal exemption only to the same extent as state bonds. That is a direct, nameable conflict between two operative provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Bonds shall bear interest at a rate determined by the commission, payable annually or semi-annually' is short and complete as amended. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.13 still caps net interest cost at six percent per annum on competitively sold issues, so the 1984 amendment freeing the rate leaves an unrepealed ceiling elsewhere. That is a specific residue of an amendment not carried through.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Place and currency of payment; entirely definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No competing provision. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Facsimile execution and the survival of signatures after officers leave; standard and precise. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 12.5 and 14.5. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short power to purchase, hold, cancel or resell its own bonds 'out of any funds available therefor'. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'Funds available therefor' must be read against 12.18's trust-fund restriction on pledged revenues, a modest interaction. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long and detailed, but with a real puzzle: bonds must be 'sold on sealed proposals to the highest bidder' while the operative constraint is expressed as a net interest cost cap, and the private-sale fallback is bounded by 'the lowest bid which was rejected' — highest bidder and lowest net interest cost are different measures. That mismatch is nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The six percent net-interest ceiling here survives the 1984 amendment of 12.9, which lets the commission set the rate; and 12.20(b) permits private placement 'notwithstanding any other provision', bypassing this whole regime. Two express escapes from a mandatory bidding rule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence negotiability rule with a single clear exception. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Fits 12.5's authorisation of coupon or registered form. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Legal investments for savings banks, fiduciaries and public funds' is a closed enumeration; whether other institutional investors are covered is an expressio unius point, but a minor one. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Applies 'in each of the signatory states' but is silent as to federal fiduciaries, consistent with 15.1's federal reservations. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Conclusive against all persons whomsoever' is a very strong preclusive phrase, and 'in rem' validation proceedings raise questions about which forum and which law applies. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It binds 'each of the signatory parties', including the United States, whereas 15.1(p) says nothing in the compact waives federal sovereign immunity from suit. That is a specific tension worth naming.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A recording exemption and a pledge-perfection rule; both are technically precise. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 12.18's lien provisions. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A very long single sentence in which the trust-fund restriction is interrupted by a lengthy 'except as and to the extent provided in the indenture' clause ending in 'or other purposes' — a catch-all that swallows the restriction it qualifies. The reference to 'all such rates, rents, tolls, fees and charges' has no clear antecedent within the section.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exclusive lien here must be reconciled with 12.6's bar on covenants restricting regulatory powers and with 3.7 and 9.5's rate-setting standards, and the antecedent for 'such rates' is really 3.7 and 12.6. The missing antecedent is a genuine drafting relationship problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Enumerated remedies followed by an express non-exclusivity sentence, which forecloses the usual expressio unius argument. Well drafted for its purpose.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'A court of competent jurisdiction of any signatory party' interacts with 15.1(p)'s federal jurisdiction grant and immunity reservation, and with New York § 634. Overlapping forums but no contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The signatory parties will provide such capital funds... as may be authorized by their respective statutes' followed by 'nothing in this section shall be deemed to impose any mandatory obligation' — the covenant is negated by its own proviso, leaving it unclear whether anything was promised. That self-cancelling structure is a real construction problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 13.3(c), by contrast, has the parties 'covenant and agree' to include apportioned amounts in their budgets (subject to their budget processes), so the compact is inconsistent about whether funding commitments bind. The 2014 WRDA endnote shows Congress had to legislate an allocation duty.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Notwithstanding any other provision of this compact' is an express override and the mechanics (private placement, optional guaranty) are clear. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overrides 12.13's mandatory competitive sale and sits against 12.3's bar on imposing bond obligations on signatory parties, though the guaranty is voluntary and constitutionally conditioned. The override is deliberate but broad.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain enabling provision for receipt of funds in any form. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 3.6(g), 14.1(a)(2) and 14.13(a); redundancy without conflict, though 15.1(e) reserves federal budgetary control. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All public and private projects and facilities which are required, in the judgment of the commission, for the optimum planning, development... of the water resources' makes the commission the judge of what 'optimum' requires, and the mandatory proviso about court decrees is a different kind of requirement bolted on. 'Optimum' and 'required' are both nameable open terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The comprehensive plan is the yardstick for Section 3.8 approval, for 11.1(b) and 11.2(b) expenditure bars, and for 5.2 and 10.5 standards, yet 15.1(s) lets the President suspend, modify or delete plan provisions — so the measure against which private projects are judged is unilaterally alterable. That interaction is a live construction problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'During the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine' fixes a number and then dissolves it in the same breath, so the six-year figure has no binding force. That self-undoing quality is a nameable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.2(b) describes the same programme with only the 'reasonably foreseeable period' formula and no six-year default, so the two statements of one duty differ. Minor but specific.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line content requirement; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Tracks 3.2(b)'s wording. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Including all public and private projects to be anticipated' is broad and undefined but is a listing requirement, not a regulatory trigger. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sweeps in 'all public and private projects' whereas 3.8 reaches only those of 'substantial effect' — the same threshold mismatch that runs through 3.2(b) and 11.2(b). Named and real, though the consequence here is only informational.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite requirement for a separate statement. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Mirrors 3.2(b)'s closing clause. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete annual capital budget requirement with specified contents. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.2(c) and 14.4(b)'s hearing requirement. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Detailed budget mechanics, but the apportionment rule — the balance 'shall be apportioned equitably among the signatory parties by unanimous vote' — combines an undefined standard ('equitably') with a unanimity requirement that gives every party a veto over its own share. That combination is a genuine construction and deadlock problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.5 sets majority voting as the default and this requires unanimity; 13.3(c)'s covenant to fund is itself subject to each party's budget process; and 15.1(e) reserves federal appropriation control, which is why WRDA 2007 and 2014 had to direct the Secretary to allocate funds. The endnote documents that the funding chain did not work as written.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Covenant and agree to include the amounts so apportioned... subject to such review and approval as may be required by their respective budgetary processes' promises payment and then makes it contingent on the promisor's own discretion — the covenant may be illusory. A named, classic defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against 12.20(a), which disclaims any mandatory funding obligation, and against 15.1(e)'s reservation of federal appropriation authority; the WRDA endnotes show Congress legislating to force allocation, confirming the covenant did not bind. Specific and documented.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem introducing auxiliary powers. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Leads a list that overlaps 3.6 and 12.20(c); redundancy only. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Enter intro contracts' is a plain typographical error for 'enter into contracts'; it is obvious and self-correcting, so it does not change meaning, but it is a mechanical mistake on the face of the text. 'Sue and be sued in all courts of competent jurisdiction' is otherwise clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York § 634 supplies a special definition of 'court of competent jurisdiction' precisely for this sub-item, and 15.1(p) grants original federal jurisdiction while reserving United States immunity — so who may sue this body, and where, is addressed in three places. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long enumeration of receivable items closing with 'and other funds, properties and services' — a catch-all after specifics, though nothing coercive turns on it. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates 3.6(g), 12.20(c) and 14.13(a) with slightly different wording each time; 15.1(e) reserves federal budget control. Redundancy, not conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete planning-and-specifications power. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps 3.9(c) and 3.6(a). Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Control and regulate the use of facilities owned or operated by the commission' is narrow and definite. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.7's rate-setting over the same facilities. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long verb-and-means string ending in 'or otherwise as it may deem necessary', a catch-all closing an enumerated list of acquisition methods. Modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It permits sale and conveyance of property while 12.18 makes pledged revenues and 12.6 the disposition of facilities subject to indenture restrictions, and 14.14/14.15 govern acquisition from public bodies. Coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All corporate powers essential to the declared objects and purposes of the commission' is a pure catch-all at the end of an enumerated list — the classic general-versus-specific structure, and 'essential' does no real limiting work. Nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates 3.6(h)'s implied-powers clause, so the compact contains two open-ended residual grants, each of which could be used to bypass the enumerated limits in Articles 4 through 11 and the reservations in 15.1. That doubling is what makes the residual grants contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem, 'subject to the provisions of this compact'. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Distinguishes commissioner functions from commission powers in (a); consistent with 2.5 and 14.5. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Except as otherwise provided by or pursuant to this compact' is a broad but conventional saving. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The phrase 'or pursuant to' lets commission rules under 14.2 reallocate the commissioners' own governing powers, a small circularity with 14.5(a)'s delegation to the executive director. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Subject to any provisions of law specifically applicable to agencies or instrumentalities created by compact' points to an unidentified and possibly empty body of law. That indeterminate referent is a nameable softness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It intersects 15.1(m)'s direction that the commission is not a federal agency for specified statutes and 15.1(n)'s denial of federal-employee status — the compact does not otherwise say what law governs it. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short internal-organisation duty. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps 2.6's self-organisation power; harmless duplication. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Appoint the principal officers' leaves 'principal' undefined. Small.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.5(a) says the commission appoints only the executive director and that 'all other officers and employees shall be appointed by the executive director' — which conflicts with a commissioner duty to appoint 'the principal officers'. That is a specific, nameable inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A broad personnel power qualified by 'subject to the provisions of this article'; concrete in subject matter. Low-moderate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is limited by 14.5(b)'s merit rule and 14.8's disqualifications, and it overlaps 14.5(a)'s allocation of appointment power to the executive director. Same tension as at 14.1(b)(4).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-word contracting power. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Constrained by 14.9's bidding rules and 14.8(c)'s voiding of tainted contracts. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare stem. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Introduces rulemaking and peace-officer powers; no conflict at the stem. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exemption from hearing and filing for rules 'which deal[] solely with the internal management of the commission' turns on the undefined word 'solely' and on where internal management ends — a nameable boundary problem in a provision that determines whether a rule is effective at all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Rules made here are enforceable by penalty under 14.17 and are the vehicle for 3.8's project-review procedure and 10.3's quantity thresholds, so whether a rule was validly adopted has instrument-wide consequences. The filing requirement also depends on five different states' administrative-procedure laws.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Vested with the powers of a peace officer of the state in which he is duly assigned' is a sweeping grant achieved by designation alone, with no limit tied to compact business. The breadth is striking but the words are clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It confers state police powers on commission employees who, under 15.1(n), are not federal officers and whose commission is, under 15.1(m), not a federal agency — the status question is unresolved instrument-wide. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The in-lieu payment formula — 'annual amounts which shall equal the taxes lawfully assessed upon property for the tax year next prior to its acquisition by the commission for a period of ten years' — is syntactically ambiguous as to whether 'for a period of ten years' modifies the payments or the assessment, and 'the payments may be thereupon terminated or continued in such reasonable amount as may be necessary or desirable' gives no standard at all. Both are nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It exempts the commission from taxation 'by or under authority of any of the signatory parties', which by 1.2(h) includes the United States, while 11.3 reserves state taxing power over withdrawals and 11.4(d)(ii) separately provides for apportioning in-lieu payments. Overlapping and partly duplicative regimes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All meetings of the commission shall be open to the public' is absolute and unqualified — no executive session, no exception for personnel or litigation. Its very absoluteness is what would be litigated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It admits no exception even for the personnel actions contemplated by 14.5, 14.8(b) and 14.11(d), or for bond negotiations under 12.13 — so read literally it is hard to reconcile with the rest of Article 14. That is a genuine whole-instrument strain.
